practice_items.prompt: In Unix, a file's owner sets read/write/execute permissions for owner, group, and others. Which access control model does this describe?
options: Discretionary Access Control (DAC)
Mandatory Access Control (MAC)
Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)
Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC)
practice_items.explain: The object's owner decides who else may access it, that discretion is the defining trait of DAC.

practice_items.prompt: Select ALL statements that correctly describe Mandatory Access Control (MAC).
options: A central policy authority assigns labels to subjects and objects
Individual object owners can freely grant access to anyone they choose
The system enforces label-based rules automatically, regardless of owner preference
MAC originated in government/military contexts (e.g., Bell-LaPadula)
practice_items.explain: MAC removes discretion from owners; enforcement is centralized and automatic based on labels.

practice_items.prompt: A hospital assigns permissions to a 'Nurse' role and a 'Billing Clerk' role rather than to each of its 5,000 staff individually. Which model is this?
options: DAC
MAC
RBAC
None of these
practice_items.explain: Permissions attached to named roles, with users assigned to roles, is Role-Based Access Control.

practice_items.prompt: Name the design principle: grant each subject only the permissions needed to do its job, nothing more.
practice_items.explain: Least privilege limits the blast radius of a compromised account.

practice_items.prompt: What is the principle that a subject should be granted only the permissions it needs to do its job, nothing more?
options: Least privilege
Separation of duties
Role recertification
Mandatory access control
practice_items.explain: Least privilege minimizes the blast radius of a compromised or misused account.

practice_items.prompt: Select ALL statements that correctly describe privilege creep.
options: It is the gradual, unnoticed accumulation of unnecessary permissions over time
It happens because missing permissions are loudly noticed and fixed, while excess permissions are silently ignored
It is prevented automatically by RBAC with no further effort
Periodic role review/recertification is used to counteract it
practice_items.explain: RBAC organizes permissions but does not by itself prevent creep; deliberate review is required.

practice_items.prompt: Why should the person who creates a vendor payment not also be the person who approves it?
options: Separation of duties requires that a sensitive process need collusion between two people to be abused
It violates least privilege by definition
Payments cannot be created and approved by the same software
It is a MAC labeling requirement
practice_items.explain: Separation of duties splits sensitive processes across roles so a single compromised or malicious account cannot complete them alone.

practice_items.prompt: Name the metaphor used to describe how much damage a compromised account with excess permissions can do.
practice_items.explain: Least privilege caps the 'blast radius' of a compromised identity.

practice_items.atom_title: Credential theft prevention and lateral movement
practice_items.prompt: An attacker who compromises one marketing laptop uses stolen credentials to hop to several other internal machines in search of valuable systems. What is this process called?
options: Lateral movement
Cross-site scripting
Broken object level authorization
Data exfiltration
practice_items.explain: Moving from an initial foothold to additional systems within the network is lateral movement.

practice_items.atom_title: Credential theft prevention and lateral movement
practice_items.prompt: Select ALL statements that correctly describe pass-the-hash / pass-the-ticket attacks.
options: The attacker authenticates using a stolen hash or ticket without ever knowing the plaintext password
These attacks require the attacker to crack the password first
They exploit authentication protocols that accept hash- or ticket-based authentication
Multi-factor authentication significantly reduces the impact of a successfully stolen credential
practice_items.explain: Pass-the-hash/ticket attacks specifically avoid needing the plaintext password; MFA blunts the value of any stolen credential.

practice_items.atom_title: Credential theft prevention and lateral movement
practice_items.prompt: Why does reusing the same local administrator password across every machine in an organization make lateral movement much easier for an attacker?
options: It has no effect on lateral movement
Shared passwords are always encrypted differently on each machine
One stolen admin credential authenticates on every machine that shares it, removing the need to steal new credentials at each hop
It only affects DAC systems
practice_items.explain: A single shared admin credential becomes a skeleton key across the whole environment once stolen.

practice_items.atom_title: Credential theft prevention and lateral movement
practice_items.prompt: Name one behavioral signal defenders watch for that suggests an account is engaged in lateral movement (e.g., unusually high count of what).
practice_items.explain: A single account authenticating to an unusually large number of distinct hosts in a short window is a classic lateral-movement signal.
